title: Products With At Least One Order
description:
Report the `name` of every product that has been ordered at least once, using `EXISTS` — not a join.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: All four products — Keyboard, Mouse, Desk and Lamp — show up in `order_items` at least once in this example (product ids 1, 2, 3 and 4 all appear across the seeded order lines), so all four pass the EXISTS check and all four are returned. A hidden test case adds a product that's never been ordered at all — its id never shows up in `order_items` no matter what, so the correlated subquery finds nothing for it and it's correctly left out.
hint: The subquery references `p.id` from the outer query — that's what makes it correlated. It's re-evaluated once per product, not once total.

title: Departments With At Least One Employee
description:
Report the `name` of every department that has at least one employee, using `EXISTS`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Engineering has Ava, Ben, Cara and Dan; Sales has Eve, Finn and Gia; HR has Hal — every one of the three departments has at least one employee, so the correlated EXISTS check passes for all three and they're all returned. A hidden test case adds a fourth department with zero employees — for that one, the subquery finds no matching row at all, EXISTS is false, and it's correctly excluded.
hint: EXISTS only cares whether the correlated subquery returns any row at all — SELECT 1 is idiomatic because the actual selected value is never used.

title: Customers With A Cancelled Order
description:
Report the `name` of every customer who has at least one order with status `cancelled`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Only one order in this data has status `cancelled` — Bo's order on 2022-02-20. Ada's three orders are all `completed`, and Cy's two orders are `completed` and `pending`; neither of them has a single cancelled order, so neither qualifies. That leaves just Bo, whose correlated subquery finds exactly that one matching row (customer_id = Bo's id, status = 'cancelled') and returns true.
hint: Both the correlation (customer_id = c.id) and the extra filter (status = 'cancelled') live inside the same subquery.

title: Out-Earning Someone In Another Department
description:
Report the `name` of every employee who earns more than **at least one** employee in a **different** department (not their own).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Seven of the eight employees qualify — only Hal is missing. Hal (HR, $60,000) is the lowest-paid person in the entire company: Sales' cheapest employee is Finn at $70,000 and Engineering's cheapest is Dan at $95,000, so there's nobody in a different department earning less than Hal — the subquery finds no match for Hal, and EXISTS is false. Everyone else clears at least one person in some other department (for example Dan at $95,000 easily out-earns HR's Hal at $60,000, even though Dan is the lowest earner within his own department).
hint: Two conditions must both hold inside the subquery: a different department AND a lower salary. Getting either condition on the wrong alias (e1 vs e2) silently breaks this.

title: Customers Whose Most Recent Order Was Cancelled
description:
For every customer, look at their single most recent order (by `order_date`). Report the `name` of every customer whose most recent order has status `cancelled`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_date = (
  SELECT MAX(o2.order_date) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = c.id
)
AND o.status = 'cancelled';
outputExplanation: Bo has exactly one order, dated 2022-02-20 with status `cancelled` — trivially both their first and their most recent order, so Bo qualifies. Ada's most recent order is on 2023-01-02 (`completed`) — even though one of her earlier orders happened to be cancelled too, that's not the *most recent* one, so she's correctly excluded. Cy's most recent order is 2022-03-06 (`pending`, not cancelled), so Cy is out too. Di has no orders at all and never even reaches the WHERE clause meaningfully. Only Bo makes it through.
hint: The correlated scalar subquery finds each customer's own latest date — compare the joined order's date against that, not against the whole table's max.

title: Above Category Average, Without A Window Function
description:
Report every product priced strictly above the average price of its own category — the same result you'd get with a window function, but written as a correlated subquery instead.

Name the columns `name`, `category` and `price`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Tech has two products: Keyboard ($80) and Mouse ($25), averaging $52.50 — Keyboard clears that average, Mouse doesn't. Furniture has Desk ($300) and Lamp ($45), averaging $172.50 — Desk clears it, Lamp doesn't. So the result is Keyboard and Desk: the pricier item in each category, but not the cheaper one. Each product's average is computed only against others in its *own* category — Keyboard is never compared against Furniture prices at all.
hint: Same idea as PARTITION BY category, just expressed as "for this row's own category, what's the average?" — recomputed once per row instead of once per partition.

title: Departments With Above-Average Headcount
description:
Considering only departments that have at least one employee, report the `name` of every department whose headcount is strictly above the average headcount across those departments.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id) >
      (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id));
outputExplanation: Engineering has 4 employees, Sales has 3, and HR has 1 — three staffed departments averaging (4 + 3 + 1) / 3 ≈ 2.67 people. Engineering's 4 and Sales' 3 both beat that average, so both are returned; HR's 1 falls well below it and is excluded. The average itself is computed once, the same for every department being compared — only the correlated headcount subquery changes per row.
hint: The first subquery is correlated (one department's own headcount); the second is not (the average headcount across all staffed departments) — mixing a correlated and a non-correlated subquery in the same WHERE clause is fine.

title: Bought Every Product In A Category
description:
Report the `name` of every customer who has ordered **every** product in the `'Tech'` category at least once. A customer who has never ordered anything does not qualify, and a customer only qualifies if the `'Tech'` category actually has at least one product.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products WHERE category = 'Tech')
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM products p
  WHERE p.category = 'Tech'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND oi.product_id = p.id
  )
);
outputExplanation: Tech has two products: Keyboard and Mouse. Ada has ordered both — Keyboard and Mouse both show up across her three orders — so there's no Tech product she's missing, and she qualifies. Cy has also ordered both, across two separate orders (Mouse in one, Keyboard in the other) — order doesn't matter, only that both eventually got ordered at some point. Bo's only order contains a Furniture item, no Tech products at all, so Bo is missing both Tech products and fails. Di has never ordered anything, so Di is trivially missing every Tech product too.
hint: This is "relational division": find customers with no Tech product they *haven't* ordered — a NOT EXISTS wrapped around another NOT EXISTS. Without the outer guard (a Tech product must exist at all), this would vacuously return every customer when the category is empty.

title: Second Highest Salary Per Department, No Window Functions
description:
For each department, find the employees earning the **second highest distinct salary** — without using any window function. Report everyone tied at that level.

Name the columns `name`, `dept_id` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id AND e2.salary > e.salary
) = 1;
outputExplanation: Engineering's distinct salaries are $150k, $120k and $95k — Ben and Cara both sit at $120k, the second tier down (only $150k, one distinct salary, beats them), so both are reported together. Sales' distinct salaries are $130k, $85k and $70k — Gia at $85k has exactly one higher distinct salary ($130k) above her, so she's the second tier there. HR has only Hal, one employee, one salary — there's no second tier to even exist, so HR contributes nothing to the result. Ava ($150k, Engineering's top) and Eve ($130k, Sales' top) are correctly excluded too: zero salaries beat theirs, not one.
hint: "Exactly one distinct salary in my own department beats mine" is precisely the definition of sitting at the second-highest tier — no DENSE_RANK required.

title: The Priciest Item In Every Order It's Part Of
description:
Report the `name` of every product that has been ordered at least once and, in **every** order it appears in, was never cheaper than any other item in that same order.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id
  AND (
    oi.unit_price IS NULL
    OR EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi2
      WHERE oi2.order_id = oi.order_id AND oi2.unit_price > oi.unit_price
    )
  )
);
outputExplanation: Keyboard ($80) appears in two orders: one where it's the only item worth more than Mouse ($25), and one where it's the sole item entirely — it's never beaten, so it qualifies. Desk ($300) and Lamp ($45) each only ever appear in orders where they're either alone or the priciest item present, so they qualify too. Mouse ($25) is the one exclusion: in the order where it appears alongside Keyboard, Keyboard's $80 beats it — so even though Mouse might be the priciest item in some *other* order, failing even once is enough to disqualify it entirely, since the rule is "every order it's part of," not "at least one."
hint: Another double negation: there is no order-line of this product where some other line in the same order costs more. A single-level NOT EXISTS would only prove "priciest in at least one order," not "priciest in every order." Watch out for NULL prices too — `NULL > x` and `x > NULL` are both unknown (never true), so without an explicit NULL check a NULL-priced item would wrongly look unbeatable.
